lessons.title: What AI is
body: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) defines an AI system as a machine-based system that works with some autonomy and infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions (Article 3(1)).

In everyday work this covers chatbots and writing assistants, translation tools, meeting transcription, CV screening, credit scoring, image generators and AI features built into office software and CRMs.
Most of these tools are trained on large amounts of data and produce the statistically likely answer. They do not understand your situation or check facts the way a person does.
points: AI is often built into tools you already use, not only separate apps.
An AI output is a suggestion produced from patterns, not a verified fact.

lessons.title: How AI fails: errors, bias and hallucination
body: Errors: AI tools can be wrong with full confidence, for example in sums, dates, names, legal or medical details, or when the question is outside what the tool was trained on.
Hallucination: generative AI can invent sources, quotes, case law, figures or product features that do not exist, and present them convincingly.
Bias: if training data under-represents or mistreats some groups, outputs can be unfair, for example in hiring, lending or translation of gendered terms.
Outdated or manipulated input: a tool may rely on old information, and hidden instructions in a web page or document (prompt injection) can steer its answer.
points: Check facts, figures and sources before you use them.
Be extra careful where an output affects a person (a candidate, a customer, a patient).
Report outputs that look wrong or unfair to the person responsible for the tool.

lessons.title: Using AI safely at work: data, confidentiality and GDPR
body: Only use AI tools your organisation has approved for the task. Free consumer versions may keep what you type and use it to improve their models.

Do not enter personal data (names, contact details, health, HR or customer records), passwords or confidential business information unless your organisation has approved that tool for that data, for example under a data processing agreement (GDPR Article 28).

The GDPR still applies when AI is involved. People have rights about decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them (GDPR Article 22). Keep a human in the loop for such decisions.
Keep a note of which AI tool helped with which piece of work when your organisation asks for it.
points: Approved tool + approved data = OK. Otherwise ask first.
Remove or anonymise personal data before you paste text.
A person reviews AI-supported decisions about people.

lessons.title: Transparency duties (Article 50)
body: Article 50 of the AI Act applies from 2 August 2026.
People must be told when they are interacting with an AI system such as a chatbot, unless that is obvious from the context (Article 50(1), a duty on providers).

Providers of generative AI must mark synthetic audio, image, video and text outputs in a machine-readable way (Article 50(2)). For systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 this applies from 2 December 2026.

Deployers must tell people when they are exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation (Article 50(3)), disclose deepfakes, and disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest unless a person has reviewed it and an editor takes responsibility (Article 50(4)).
points: Customer-facing chatbot? Make sure it says it is an AI.
Publishing AI-generated images, video or audio that look real? Label them.
Ask the tool owner if you are unsure whether a disclosure is in place.

lessons.title: What Article 4 requires
body: Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025. National authorities supervise and enforce it from August 2026.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since 27 July 2026) replaced the wording. Article 4(1) now says that providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context of use, and the people the systems are used on.

It adds: this obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. The Commission and the Member States must support these efforts, in particular for SMEs (Article 4(2)), and the AI Board adopts recommendations (Article 4(3)).

No certificate or exam is required. The Commission's AI literacy Q&A says organisations can keep an internal record of trainings and other guiding initiatives. A course like this one is one possible measure; your organisation decides what fits.
points: The duty is on the organisation (provider or deployer), to take measures that fit.
There is no fixed level and no mandatory certificate.
A simple record of who did what training, and when, is sensible evidence.

lessons.title: Roles: provider, deployer and you
body: Provider: develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name (Article 3(3)).
Deployer: uses an AI system under its authority in a professional activity (Article 3(4)). A business that uses a chatbot, a translation tool or an AI writing assistant at work is a deployer.
Importers and distributors have their own duties when they bring AI systems onto the EU market. Purely personal, non-professional use falls outside the deployer role.
You: as staff or a contractor working on the organisation's behalf, you are one of the people Article 4 is about. Your organisation supports your AI literacy; you apply it in daily work.
points: Most businesses are deployers of the AI tools they buy.
A business that builds AI into its own product can also be a provider.
Know who in your organisation owns each AI tool.

lessons.title: Your everyday checklist
body: Before: is this tool approved for this task and this data?
During: do not paste personal or confidential data unless approved; give clear instructions; keep the context in mind.
After: check facts, sources and fairness; add a disclosure where one is needed; a person decides when the output affects someone.

Later dates to know: high-risk rules apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III uses such as recruitment and credit scoring, and from 2 August 2028 for AI in regulated products (Annex I), as set by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
points: When in doubt, ask the tool owner or your manager.

quiz.q: Under the AI Act, which description best fits an AI system?
o: A machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content or decisions

quiz.q: A generative AI tool gives you a case reference that you cannot find anywhere. What is the most likely explanation?
o: It may be a hallucination: an invented reference

quiz.q: Where is AI bias most harmful?
o: Decisions about people, such as hiring or lending

quiz.q: You want to summarise a customer complaint that contains the customer's name and address. What should you do?
o: Paste it into any free chatbot
Use only a tool approved for that data, or remove the personal data first
E-mail it to a friend to summarise

quiz.q: Which GDPR article gives people rights about decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them?
From when do the Article 50 transparency duties apply?
Your website chatbot answers customers. What does Article 50(1) require?
o: People are told they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious
The chatbot must be switched off at night

quiz.q: Since 27 July 2026, what does Article 4(1) require of providers and deployers?
o: To guarantee a set level of AI literacy for each person
To take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and others acting on their behalf
To send every employee to an EU exam

quiz.q: Does the AI Act require staff to hold an AI literacy certificate?
o: No; an internal record of trainings and other measures is a sensible approach

quiz.q: A shop uses a third-party AI chatbot on its website. What is the shop's role?
According to Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, from when do high-risk rules apply to Annex III uses such as recruitment?
